title: Prayer times in the far north
word: Prayer times in the far north
hook: where the sun barely sets, scholars give rulings for prayer and fasting

segments.voice: Yesterday, moon sighting debates, and Kurayb coming home from Syria. Your line was one moon, many views. How does your community decide? Today, the sun gets difficult too. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-five.

Midsummer, somewhere far north. It's late in the evening and the sky is still bright. A family has been fasting since before dawn, and dawn came early, because night never quite arrived. The table is set. The dates are out. Someone keeps checking the window. The sun touches the horizon, slides along it, and seems unwilling to go. The question at that table is an old one in a new place. When the Qur'an says fast until night, and the night barely comes, what do you do? Today: the rulings for prayer and fasting where the sun won't keep the usual hours.
screen: `A TABLE SET, A SKY STILL BRIGHT.` → `THE SUN WON'T GO.` → `WHEN NIGHT BARELY COMES.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an ties the fast to the sky. In Pickthall's translation, the believers may "eat and drink until the white thread becometh distinct to you from the black thread of the dawn. Then strictly observe the fast till nightfall." Dawn and nightfall. The daily prayers are tied to the sun's movements the same way. In Mecca and Medina, the sun keeps steady hours. Far north, in summer, the dawn light may never fully fade, and in winter the day may hardly come. Scholars turn to a report in Sahih Muslim. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, spoke of a time to come when a day would be as long as a year. His companions asked the obvious question: will one day's prayers be enough for that day? He said no; estimate its measure, and pray accordingly. So the principle is already there: when the sun stops being a usable clock, you measure. How to measure is where the views differ. Some scholars say to follow the times of the nearest place where day and night are still clearly distinct. Some say to follow the times of Mecca. Some say that if the long fast can be kept, keep it by your own sky, and use an estimate only when the signs disappear or the strain becomes too great. Behind all of them stands a line from the close of the same chapter, in Pickthall's words: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." The family at the window isn't facing a gap in their religion. They're standing exactly where a question was asked and answered: estimate its measure.
screen: `DAWN AND NIGHTFALL SET THE FAST.` · `A DAY AS LONG AS A YEAR.` · `ESTIMATE ITS MEASURE.` · `NEAREST PLACE, MECCA, OR YOUR OWN SKY.` · then, large: `NOT BEYOND ITS SCOPE.`

segments.voice: The practice: think of Muslims near the poles. Settle, and breathe. Picture that kitchen far north, the light still coming through the window late at night, the table waiting. Picture someone on a winter morning there, praying in the dark before a sun that will barely rise. Hold them both for a few breaths, people keeping the same prayers as everyone else under a sky that won't cooperate. If you pray, you can keep them in your prayers. If you don't, simply let your own sky, whatever it's doing right now, feel a little more ordinary and a little more of a gift. The bell holds the time.
Prayer times in the far north. Where the sun barely sets or barely rises, scholars estimate the times for prayer and fasting. Today's word.
screen: `PRAYER TIMES IN THE FAR NORTH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: ramadan under the midnight sun. Today, notice when your own sun rises and sets, and think of those who have to estimate it. Tomorrow, refugees and the Hijra. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Muslims living far north follow rulings from scholars and local councils: some pray and fast by the times of the nearest place with a clear day and night, some by the times of Mecca, and some by their own sky when the signs can still be seen.

fork.setup: you're one of the companions. the Prophet has just described a day as long as a year. you ask: will one day's prayers be enough for it? what does he answer?
options: yes, the usual prayers once for the whole long day.
no; estimate its measure and pray accordingly.
